doc.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
title: Swing, bebop and jump bands on the same bill
summary: Styles shared bills until booking agents separated them; Louis Jordan influenced Parker.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You talked about touring, some of the bands that you’ve played with, and a sense of the emerging new music. But it was also a time in which you could, as you cited with dances – you’d hear the swing. You’d hear the more advanced modern music. And if there’s a Louis Jordan there, you’re hearing something else. You’re hearing jump swing or some other variation, some other genre. Then you do things later in your career, like with Buddy Johnson, with Lloyd Price, even Motown, because as time goes on, the separations between the musics are more definite. You don’t find them on the same bill, played by the same musicians, as close – the branches are more separate. In your mind, as a musician, particularly in the mid-’50s as you developed your career, were these things separate? Or not?

Especially in the ’40s and ’50s, you would find some of these bands on the same bill. You’d find Dizzy’s band on the same bill with one of the swing bands, because people didn’t find it necessary to separate them. That came later. Everything started becoming more separate later, because the people that were in – the booking agents wanted to separate the things, so that they could finally have control over something. But all of those musics have a lot in it that’s related. Louis Jordan played a lot of things that must have sounded – that must have influenced Charlie Parker in his own improvsations.
